prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions make credit and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, generating credit cycles and persistent macroeconomic fluctuations

statement.case_for: My configuration changed in one respect: B006 is now a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize, not the three-name version I proposed in round 1. The case rests on the collateral-amplification mechanism in Kiyotaki and Moore (1997), 'Credit cycles', and on its later extensions in Kiyotaki and Moore (2002, 'Balance-sheet contagion'; 2019, liquidity and business cycles). It is a single, well-bounded discovery. Collateral values and credit limits feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent. The idea is about thirty years old, was tested by 2007-09, and is part of the shared core of macro, finance and central-bank modelling. Timing is not a concern. The reasons for dropping Gertler are the chair's questions and my own re-examination. I tried to name the papers that carry a separable Gertler claim. The Bernanke-Gertler and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator papers overlap with Bernanke's 2022 recognition. Gertler and Karadi (2011) on unconventional policy involves a co-author outside the credited names. Gertler and Kiyotaki (2010, handbook chapter) and Gertler and Kiyotaki (2015, bank runs) are the best remaining candidates. The 2015 paper is about bank runs, which is the theme closest to the 2022 prize. That leaves a thin and contestable independent credit, and a citation could not describe it without either re-recognising adjacent work or overstating it. The two-name award credits the originating mechanism cleanly. I recall these papers from general knowledge, not from verified source data. I keep B006 ahead of B047 on breadth of use across macro theory, quantitative models and policy practice, but I regard that margin as small and a matter of weighting, not a decisive scientific difference.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic proximity to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I argue that collateral amplification in the real economy is a distinct discovery from bank runs and deposit insurance, but the committee could reasonably treat the two as adjacent and judge that the field has been recently recognised. The empirical identification of the specific collateral channel is mixed, and the evidence is stronger for financial amplification in general than for the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism. A two-name award also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose quantitative and empirical work made the framework policy-usable. Some of that credit is real and goes unrecognised under this configuration. Finally, B047 has a comparably clean three-name core and no recent recognition of its field, and B047 has a stronger direct record of use in policy practice. As an industrial organisation economist I may be biased in either direction on B047, and I cannot rule out that I weigh it incorrectly.

responses.point: Hassler's current round-1 file proposes Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He ties Gertler's credit to the intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki and to quantitative financial-friction models, not to the accelerator papers. He wants the citation to name collateral constraints and balance-sheet frictions and to exclude bank runs and deposit insurance, which the 2022 prize addressed.
responses.response: I made the same argument in round 1, and I now think it is harder to sustain than we suggested. When I tried to name the papers that carry the Gertler claim, the best candidates were the Gertler-Kiyotaki handbook chapter, the Gertler-Karadi unconventional-policy model and the Gertler-Kiyotaki bank-runs paper. The first is largely a survey and synthesis of existing mechanisms. The second involves a co-author outside the credited names. The third is on bank runs, the theme you rightly want kept out of the citation. A citation that excludes bank runs therefore also shrinks Gertler's separable credit. I agree with you that the committee should say openly that the accelerator credit is partly absorbed. I draw the conclusion that the pair is the cleaner configuration, and I have moved to it. I recognise that this differs from your own current three-name proposal.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and would back a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version of B006. He argues that even with clean attribution the 2022 overlap makes B006 less of a new step than a field with no recent recognition, and that the empirical record on the collateral channel is a weaker evidentiary base than BLP's decades of applied use.
responses.response: The two-name configuration meets part of your objection on attribution, and I think your agreement that it is the defensible version is useful. I do not agree that overlap with 2022 makes it less of a new step. The 2022 prize recognised the theory of bank runs and the empirical cost of banking crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values and credit limits propagate shocks through firms and households in the real economy. These are different discoveries, though the citation must be worded carefully so that the difference is visible. I do accept your evidence point. The identification of the specific collateral channel is weaker than the evidence behind BLP, and I do not hide that. My view is that a mechanism can be prize-worthy if it organised a large research programme and survived the 2008 test, even if the channel is not settled in every micro-data detail. That is a weighting choice and I do not claim it is decisive.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B047 with Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. He argues that it is a compact, mature method whose use in merger review, antitrust and regulation shows demonstrated influence. He also argues that the omission of Bresnahan and Reiss is a real cost of the three-name cap and not something to fix by enlarging the prize. He names the two-name B006 as the alternative he would most readily support.
responses.response: I agree with you on how to treat the Bresnahan-Reiss omission. Their entry and market-structure work is a distinct and earlier tradition, so enlarging the BLP trio would dilute attribution. My own view is that the cost is real. I would add that the omission is of the same kind as Gertler's under B006, because each is a cost of a clean core under a three-person cap, so neither ballot gains on attribution cost. Your statement that the pair is the version of B006 you would most readily support is the most informative thing in the exchange for me, because it tells me where our difference actually lies. It is mainly on breadth across fields versus a methodological toolkit, and I concede that this is close. I keep B047 as my first alternative, and I have tried not to let my proximity to IO lead me to either over-weight or under-weight it.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B006 first and says the third name is an open question. He would accept the Kiyotaki-Moore pair and would not hold up the award on that point. He keeps B047 as his first alternative, noting that BLP's impact is concentrated in IO and adjacent applied fields while financial-friction mechanisms are part of the core of macro, finance and policy modelling.
responses.response: I share your reasoning on breadth and I think we have reached the same fallback. I would add a caution to my own argument. Breadth of use across fields is a legitimate common criterion, but it is partly a function of how many people work in the receiving fields. Antitrust and merger review are narrower in the number of researchers than macro-finance but have direct policy consequences in practice. I therefore treat the B006 margin over B047 as small. On the evidence you would want to settle it, my view is that the sensitivity of BLP markups and merger counterfactuals to functional form, and the validation of collateral predictions in micro data, are both partial. I do not think either can be settled by the committee from background knowledge, and this is the main reason my confidence in the ordering is limited.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the collateral-amplification mechanism as distinct enough from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which is the main factor that could move B006 below B047 or B023.

Whether Gertler's separable credit is larger than I now judge. My attempt to name supporting papers rests on recollection of Gertler-Kiyotaki and Gertler-Karadi, not on verified source or citation data.
How to weigh B006 against B047 on breadth of use versus demonstrated policy use. I regard the margin as small and cannot settle it from the shortlist alone.

How sensitive BLP markup and merger counterfactuals are to functional-form and equilibrium assumptions, and how well the collateral channel is validated in micro data. I rely on general knowledge for both.

Whether a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore award attracts or loses support relative to a three-name version. I do not treat support counts as evidence of merit, and I have changed my configuration for the attribution reasons given.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. None of Kiyotaki and Moore, nor the alternatives' credited names (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes; Mian, Sufi, Campbell), appears among my listed co-authors or institutional ties in the supplied profile. I have co-authored with committee chair Hassler and former chair Ellingsen (IJIO 2026). Hassler is a B006 supporter. Ellingsen is not a credited candidate. I disclose this without adjudicating it. My field of industrial organisation is closest to B047, which is my first alternative, and I have tried to apply the same maturity and attribution criteria to B006 and B047. I am also an SSE colleague of several committee members. As a public fact only, my spouse is a Swedish politician. The profile gives no evidence that this bears on any candidate or on my committee work.
